about: Programming 1 and 2 of TU Wien's Institut für Mikroelektronik, taught in C in 2015 with the course book Klima and Selberherr (2010), Programmieren in C, 3rd edition, Springer, cited by section and printed page; the lecture slides of Ceric et al. (2015) follow the book. The last lab compares how C, C++, Java, Python and JavaScript give memory back; each rule there is quoted from that language's own documentation, checked on 2 Nov 2026 (bibliography.json). The course left question catalogues but no worked exercises: practice answers are the book's own worked examples where it gives them, otherwise worked by hand, and say which.

lectures.title: Searching, sorting and the heap structure
Data structures: lists, search trees and hashes
Pointers, the stack and dynamic memory
Who gives memory back: C, C++, Java, Python, JavaScript

labs.title: Sequential and binary search
labs.idea: To find a number, look at one element after another, or, if the array is sorted, look in the middle and throw away the half that cannot hold it. Halving needs only about log₂ N looks.

labs.title: Bubble sort and quicksort
labs.idea: Bubble sort compares neighbours and swaps them until no swap is left. Quicksort puts one element in its final place, smaller ones to its left and larger to its right, and sorts both sides the same way.
labs.law: QuickSort(l, r): pos = Positioniere(l, r); QuickSort(l, pos − 1); QuickSort(pos + 1, r)

lawWhere.means: sorts feld between the bounds l and r by calling itself on both parts (§ 18.3.2, p. 262)

the index where Positioniere placed the element (p. 262)
left and right bound of the part to sort, indices (§ 18.3.2, p. 262)

equations.note: bubble sort's step; sorted when a pass makes no swap

where.means: the array being sorted (§ 13.6.2, p. 172)

equations.note: one pass of Positioniere with the rightmost element, 3, as the one placed

practice.question: One pass of Positioniere on 6 4 7 9 1 5 2 8 3 places the 3. At which index (from 0) does it end up?
practice.solution: The pass gives 2 1 3 9 4 5 6 8 7: the 3 stands at index 2, with only 2 and 1 to its left.

practice.question: After bubble sort's first pass over 6 4 8 3 2, which number stands last?
practice.solution: The largest number rises to the end in the first pass: 4 6 3 2 8.

labs.title: The heap: a tree in an array
labs.idea: A heap keeps the largest key at the top of a complete binary tree stored in an array. A new key climbs up (UpHeap); after the top is removed, the last key sinks down (DownHeap). Removing the top again and again sorts.

lawWhere.means: the array the heap is stored in (§ 19.5.1, p. 287)
position of a node, counted from 1 as in the book: its children are at 2i and 2i + 1, its parent at i/2 (p. 288)
rounding down, as C's integer division (the book's i/2, p. 288)

equations.eq: children of i: 2i and 2i + 1; parent: i/2
equations.note: the tree is kept in an array without links; positions counted from 1, as in the book

where.means: position of a node in the array, counted from 1 (p. 288)
rounding down: the book's integer division i/2 (p. 288)

equations.note: the heap condition

where.means: the node's key (Schlüssel) (p. 287)
a node and its successor (Nachfolger) in the tree (p. 287)

practice.question: Insert 5, 9, 3, 12 and 7, in this order, into an empty heap. Which key is at the top?
practice.solution: Each new key climbs while its parent is smaller; the largest, 12, ends at the top: 12 9 3 5 7.

labs.title: The linked list: order kept in links
labs.idea: A list stores its elements and, separately, their order: each node holds an element and a link to the next node, and the head names the first. Inserting or removing changes one or two links and moves nothing, but finding a place means walking from the head.

practice.question: The list L I S T E of Fig. 19.4 is in array cells 0 to 4. ListeEinfuegen(feld, &kopf, 5, 3) inserts N from cell 5. At which place in the list does N now stand, counted from 1?
practice.source: Klima and Selberherr (2010), pp. 270–271: the call is the book's; the place worked by hand
practice.solution: Position 3 means after the third node: the walk goes L, I, S, then N is linked in after S. The list reads L I S N T E, so N is fourth, although it sits in array cell 5.

labs.title: Binary search trees: shape from order
labs.idea: In a binary search tree every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree larger; equal keys go left. Searching and inserting go down one path. The order in which keys are inserted decides the shape: the same keys can make a bushy tree of few levels or a chain as slow as a list.

practice.question: Insert E I N B E I S P I E L, in this order, into an empty binary search tree (Fig. 19.21). How many nodes does a search for N compare?
practice.source: Klima and Selberherr (2010), p. 283: N is greater than E, greater than I, then found
practice.solution: The tree is Fig. 19.18. N > E: go right to I; N > I: go right to N; found. Three nodes: E, I and N.

practice.question: How many levels has a complete binary tree of 11 nodes?
practice.solution: log₂ 11 ≈ 3.46; its whole part is 3, plus 1 gives 4 levels.

labs.title: Hash tables: an index from the key
labs.idea: A hash function turns a key into an array index 0 … N − 1, so a search goes straight to one cell. Keys that collide share a list in that cell (separate chaining). Searching then costs a few comparisons along one short list, as long as the array is long enough and the keys spread evenly.

the length of the array; best a prime (p. 297)

practice.question: Wald, Wiese, Dorf, Bach and Holz are inserted, in this order, into a hash of length 11 with separate chaining (Fig. 19.34). How many comparisons does an unsuccessful search take on average?
practice.solution: The lists have lengths 0 0 1 0 0 3 0 0 1 0 0 (Table 19.2: 5, 2, 5, 8, 5). An unsuccessful search reads a whole list: 5/11 ≈ 0.45.

practice.question: In the same hash, how many comparisons does a successful search take on average?
practice.solution: New records go to the head of their list, so list 5 reads Holz, Dorf, Wald. The places are 1 (Wiese), 1 (Bach), 1, 2 and 3: (1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 1)/5 = 1.6.

labs.title: Pointers and pointer arithmetic
labs.idea: A pointer holds an address. Adding n moves it on by n elements, not n bytes: ptr + n is the address of feld[n].

labs.title: The program stack
labs.idea: Each call puts a frame with its own local variables on the stack; each return takes it off. A recursive function stacks one frame per open call.

lawWhere.means: the function Faktorielle (§ 18.2, p. 258)
a whole number, N in the book; the recursion ends at N = 0 with 0! = 1, (18.2), p. 257

equations.eq: call: push a frame; return: pop it
equations.note: the program stack, managed by the operating system, holds the local variables of functions

practice.question: How many frames of factorial are on the stack at most while factorial(5) runs?
practice.solution: factorial(5) calls 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 before any returns: six frames at once, as Fig. 18.2 shows (N = 5 down to N = 0).

labs.title: malloc, realloc and free
labs.idea: Memory from malloc lives on the heap until free gives it back; nobody frees it for you. Lose the last pointer and it leaks; free it twice or use it after free and the behaviour is undefined.

equations.note: the length is in bytes, not elements; 0 when no memory is free

where.means: length of the block asked for, in bytes [B] (§ 20.2, p. 304)

equations.note: many systems round blocks up to a multiple of 8 bytes
other pointers into the old block become invalid
freeing twice can crash the program; free(0) does nothing

where.means: pointer to a block from malloc, calloc or realloc (the book's db, § 20.4, p. 308)

practice.question: On a system that rounds blocks up to multiples of 8 bytes, how many bytes does malloc(10) take?
practice.solution: The next multiple of 8 above 10 is 16.

labs.title: Who gives memory back
labs.idea: The same situations in five languages: C waits for free, C++ frees when the owner ends, CPython frees most objects as soon as nothing refers to them, Java and JavaScript free what is no longer reachable when their collector runs.
labs.law: manual (C) · ownership (C++) · reference counting (CPython) · tracing (Java, JavaScript)
labs.lecture: C: Klima and Selberherr (2010), ch. 20; C++: cppreference; Java: JVM Specification SE 21, § 2.5.3; Python: Language Reference, § 3.1; JavaScript: MDN

equations.eq: C: free returns the block; free twice is undefined
equations.note: deallocates space from malloc, calloc or realloc; a null pointer does nothing

equations.eq: C++: unique_ptr disposes of its object when destroyed or reset
equations.note: the object goes when its owner does

equations.eq: Java: never explicitly deallocated; reclaimed by a garbage collector
equations.note: heap storage for objects is reclaimed by automatic storage management

equations.eq: Python: reference counting with delayed detection of cycles (CPython)
equations.note: most objects go as soon as they are unreachable; cycles wait for the detector; other implementations differ
unreachable means no longer needed; cycles are no problem; no modern engine uses reference counting
